lesson.title: Putting Things in Order: Standard Form of a Polynomial
lesson.summary: Standard form arranges a polynomial's terms from highest degree to lowest degree, so the leading term, the degree, and the overall structure are all visible at a glance.
lesson.body:
A polynomial can be written with its terms in any order without changing its value, since addition can happen in any sequence. Standard form is simply the agreed upon convention for writing polynomials consistently: terms are arranged starting with the highest degree and working down to the lowest, ending with the constant term if there is one. Finding the degree of each term, exactly as covered earlier, is the only tool needed to put a polynomial into this order.

Take the polynomial 5x - 3x^4 + 7 + 2x^3, written in a scattered, non standard order. First identify the degree of every term: 5x has degree 1, -3x^4 has degree 4, 7 has degree 0, and 2x^3 has degree 3. Now arrange the terms from highest degree to lowest: degree 4, then 3, then 1, then 0. That gives the standard form -3x^4 + 2x^3 + 5x + 7.

Rearranging terms does not change what the polynomial equals, only how it looks, so the two versions must evaluate identically for any input. Checking at x = 1, the original gives 5(1) - 3(1)^4 + 7 + 2(1)^3 = 5 - 3 + 7 + 2 = 11. The standard form gives -3(1)^4 + 2(1)^3 + 5(1) + 7 = -3 + 2 + 5 + 7 = 11. Both equal 11, confirming that reordering the terms produced an equivalent expression.

Let's put one more polynomial in standard form: 6 - x^3 + 4x^5 - 2x. Checking degrees, 6 has degree 0, -x^3 has degree 3, 4x^5 has degree 5, and -2x has degree 1. Arranging from highest degree to lowest gives 4x^5 - x^3 - 2x + 6. Checking at x = 1, the original gives 6 - 1 + 4 - 2 = 7, and the standard form gives 4 - 1 - 2 + 6 = 7, confirming the two versions are equivalent. Occasionally a problem will ask for ascending order instead, which simply reverses the pattern, listing terms from lowest degree to highest, but unless a problem specifically asks for that, descending order is what standard form means by default.

Standard form also makes it easy to spot missing degrees. In the polynomial 4x^5 - x^3 - 2x + 6 written above, there is no x^4 or x^2 term at all; those degrees simply do not appear, since a term with a coefficient of 0 is not written out. When adding this polynomial to another one, it can help to mentally note that its x^4 and x^2 coefficients are 0, so that no term from the other polynomial gets missed when matching up like terms by degree.

When a polynomial involves more than one variable, standard form is usually built around one chosen main variable, with terms ordered by that variable's degree, and any ties broken by a second variable if needed. This lesson focuses on the single variable case, which is by far the most common situation you will meet at this stage.

Standard form is more than just tidiness. With terms sorted by degree, the leading term sits in the first position automatically, so the leading coefficient and the overall degree can be read off immediately without hunting through the whole expression. It also makes adding and subtracting polynomials far more reliable, since matching degree terms from two different polynomials line up in a predictable way, much like lining up digits by place value before adding large numbers, which is exactly the skill covered next.
